newsitem.title: USA: Doctors spot telltale signs of eastern equine encephalitis.
newsitem.headline: Doctors spot telltale signs of eastern equine encephalitis.

text.p: Telltale abnormalities in an area deep in the brain can help doctors reach a faster diagnosis on the deadly disease eastern equine encephalitis or EEE, according to a study issued on Wednesday.
Researchers from Brigham and Women's Hospital examined the brain scans of 33 patients for signs of EEE, a disease carried by mosquitoes which can cause seizures and even death.

They found that the best technique for finding the abnormalities in an area of the brain known as the basal ganglia was to use magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans. MRIs use magnetism and radio waves to take cross-sectional images of the body.

"Diagnosing this rare disease is difficult for clinicians because symptoms are nonspecific, often resembling herpes simplex encephalitis," lead researcher Dr. Robert Deresiewicz said in the New England Journal of Medicine.

Although no good treatment for the disease exists and about one-third of the people who get it die, a quick diagnosis can help public health officials pinpoint the source of the infection "and mosquito control measures (can be) initiated," he said.

Between 1955 and 1993, 223 cases of EEE were reported to the Centres for Disease Control and Prevention in Atlanta. The early symptoms of the disease, including fever, headache and cramps, usually evolve into confusion, weakness and seizures.
